abstract: Feed-forward models accurately estimate camera motion and 3D geometry from short video windows. However, computational and memory costs prevent direct inference on sequences containing thousands of frames. Long videos must therefore be processed as overlapping chunks. This division produces independent local reconstructions with inconsistent coordinate frames and duplicate estimates of shared cameras. Achieving global consistency requires propagating constraints from adjacent overlaps and distant revisits across the sequence. This requirement naturally motivates pose graph optimization. However, the choice of graph level creates a trade-off. Chunk-level graphs efficiently resolve scale drift and close large loops. Yet, their rigid transformations cannot correct internal errors or conflicting frame predictions. Conversely, frame-level optimization offers local flexibility, but scaling it globally is computationally expensive and can break metric scale. HiP3R resolves this trade-off using a hierarchical pose graph. HiP3R first optimizes a robust chunk-level $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ graph to establish the global layout and scale. It then holds this layout fixed and estimates one shared $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ camera per frame, turning overlapping window predictions into a single trajectory. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of HiP3R in improving camera trajectories and 3D reconstruction. Our method applies to both chunk-based and streaming backends without additional training or fine-tuning.

sections.body: The section motivates the problem. Feed-forward models handle short clips, so long videos are split into overlapping chunks. Each chunk gives an independent reconstruction with its own coordinate frame, and shared cameras get duplicate estimates. Chunk-level similarity alignment corrects scale and orientation drift, but it cannot fix conflicting frame predictions within overlaps. The proposed HiP3R uses a chunk-level $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ graph for layout and then a frame-level shared-camera graph. Across seven benchmarks, the authors report better trajectory accuracy than loop-enabled VGGT-Long under matched backends and windows. Figure 1 illustrates the frame-level conflict.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Long videos processed in overlapping chunks yield inconsistent frame poses that chunk-level alignment alone cannot fix.

sections.body: Related work covers three areas. Feed-forward models such as DUSt3R, MASt3R and VGGT regress pointmaps from image sets, but quadratic attention restricts them to short windows. Streaming and recurrent models, including CUT3R, StreamVGGT and LingBot-MAP, process frames causally but still accumulate drift on long trajectories. Chunk-based methods such as VGGT-Long and VGGT-Align align adjacent chunks with pairwise similarity transforms, and the authors state that a rigid similarity per chunk cannot resolve overlapping-frame disagreements. HiP3R is positioned as post-processing that adds global loops and per-frame pose consistency without retraining, and without optimizing 3D tracks.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior long-video methods use chunk-level alignment or streaming memory, and this work adds global loops and per-frame consistency as post-processing.

sections.body: The method uses frozen backend outputs in two stages. Stage I builds a chunk-level similarity graph from overlap edges and loop edges. Each chunk holds a similarity transform, and loop constraints are added in order of increasing temporal span, with Huber loss and per-edge confidence weights. Stage II keeps that layout fixed and optimizes one rigid camera per frame. It combines within-chunk relative motion factors with placement priors from every chunk that observes the frame. Long sequences use a keyframe subgraph, and interpolated corrections recover the remaining frames. Appendix D gives the solver settings. This section reports no quantitative results.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: A two-stage pose graph first fits chunk similarities with loop closures, then optimizes one shared camera per frame.

sections.body: Evaluation uses seven public benchmarks with 61 sequences, including indoor sets (7-Scenes, Neural RGB-D), ETH3D, Tanks and Temples, and outdoor sets (Oxford Spires, KITTI, VBR). Metrics are ATE, relative rotation and translation errors, pairwise pose AUC, and Chamfer distance with F1. With VGGT-Omega, Table 1 reports macro ATE falling from 18.555 to 4.906 m and RPErot from 1.820 to 0.590 degrees. Table 2 shows that loop closures cut VGGT-Long ATE on KITTI from 110.3 to 10.19 m, while HiP3R reaches 9.730 m. On VBR, HiP3R gives 22.44 m against 41.27 m with loops. Table 3 reports Chamfer falling from 0.0759 to 0.0272 m. The authors note that native VGGT-Omega already reaches ATE of 0.037 m and 0.019 m on 7-Scenes and Neural RGB-D, which leaves little room for correction.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Across seven benchmarks, HiP3R reduces macro trajectory error from 18.555 to 4.906 m with VGGT-Omega and from 8.288 to 4.017 m with LingBot-MAP.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the method. A chunk-level similarity graph recovers layout and scale, then a shared-camera SE(3) graph refines trajectories with the chunk transforms held fixed. The authors claim better overall trajectory accuracy and surface reconstruction with both VGGT-Omega and LingBot-MAP on indoor and outdoor benchmarks. They state that distant loop closures correct accumulated drift while reconciling conflicting predictions across windows. Two open directions are named: extending the hierarchy to online updates, and improving its handling of unreliable loop closures. No new experiments appear in this section.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: HiP3R improves trajectory and surface accuracy on indoor and outdoor benchmarks, while online updates and unreliable loop closures remain open.

sections.body:
The appendix contains supporting derivations, settings and ablations.

- Appendix B gives closed-form Jacobian blocks for SE(3) residuals. On a 735-frame scene, graph coloring substantially cut post-processing time compared with finite differences.
- Appendix C defines the keyframe subgraph, with a default stride of 5 for sequences over 2000 frames.
- Appendix D lists solver settings, and Appendix E lists dataset compositions and splits.
- Appendix F reports stage-wise runtimes.
- Appendix L and Table 20 cover placement and motion ablations and layout-solver components. One test perturbs 25% of loop edges with a 10 degree rotation error.
- Appendix M extends dense geometry results across optimization stages.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix covers Jacobian derivations, keyframe subgraph rules, solver settings, dataset splits, runtimes, and ablations on loop noise and placement.
